and periodically driven dynamics experimentally for a single photon that its
coupled to its environment. We develop a comprehensive theory which explains
the experimental observations and offers an analytical characterization of the
non-equilibrium steady states of the system. We demonstrate that the periodic
driving and the properties of the environment can be engineered in such a way
that there is asymptotically non-vanishing bidirectional information flow
between the open system and the environment.
  Interestingly, the experimental observations and the theoretical analysis
show that, if the driving is sufficient strong, the non-equilibrium steady state
can be preferred to ascribe it to a quantum nonequilibrium dynamic, if the
driving is not strong enough, and certain asymptotic values of the evolution
variables are reached from classical balance between the system and the
environment, alike to what happens in closed quantum systems. That is, the
strength of the driving determines whether open quantum system or a closed
quantum system is being observed.
  We show that the asymptotic values of the open system can be explained from
a quantum balance condition involving the time-averaged Hamiltonian, the
environment, and the driving. This allows us to identify whether the periodic
driven dynamics can be regarded as an open quantum system or as a closed one,
depending on the range of values that the balance condition can be satisfied. This
balance condition is similar to the quantum adiabatic condition, but it is valid
for any rate of change of the parameters.
  Finally, we show that if the driving is sufficiently strong, the quantum
balance condition is satisfied and the nonequilibrium steady state is reached
very efficiently, without need of large dissipation. This allows us to design
procedures to prepare non-equilibrium steady states, that could be of practical
use in quantum technology.
  In conclusion, we report a comprehensive characterization of periodically
driven and time discrete photon dynamics, and we demonstrate that the dynamics
can be explained from a balance between the photon and the environment, which
is the same balance that closes in closed quantum systems. This balance can be
used to prepare non-equilibrium steady states without need of large dissipation
and it can be of practical use in quantum technology.

Numeration in base p/q is defined by a function
that evaluates each finite word over A_p={0,1,...,p-1} to some rational number.
We let N_p/q denote the image of this evaluation function. In particular, N_p/q
contains all nonnegative integers and the literature on base p/q usually
focuses on the set of words that are evaluated to nonnegative integers; it is a
rather chaotic language which is not context-free. On the contrary, we study
here the subsets of (N_p/q)^d that are p/q-recognisable, i.e. realised by
finite automata over (A_p)^d. First, we give a characterisation of these sets
as those definable in a first-order logic, similar to the one given by the
B\"uchi-Bruy\`ere Theorem for integer bases numeration systems. Second, we show
that the natural order relation and the modulo-q operator are not
p/q-recognisable.
  We also give sufficient conditions for a product of recognisable sets to be
recognisable, and we use them to describe the structure of the sets
p/q-recognisable as a subfamily of star-free sets^(N_p/q).
  Finally, we study the particular case of length-2 words. We give a complete
description of the length-2 p/q-recognisable sets, and we show a connection
between this base/q numeration system and the binary numeration system.
Moreover, we find a characterisation of the p/q-recognisable sets of length 2 as
the union of two subfamily of star-free sets^(N_p/q), similar to the one given
for integer bases numeration systems by the B\"uchi-Bruy\`ere Theorem.

Edges and boundaries encode shape information, while textures manifest the
appearance of regions. Despite the success of Convolutional Neural Networks
(CNNs) in computer vision and medical image analysis applications,
predominantly only texture abstractions are learned, which often leads to
imprecise boundary delineations. In medical imaging, expert manual segmentation
often relies on organ boundaries; for example, to manually segment a liver, a
medical practitioner usually identifies edges first and subsequently fills in
the segmentation mask. Motivated by these observations, we propose a
plug-and-play module, dubbed Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), that can be used with
existing encoder-decoder architectures to process both edge and texture
information. The EG-CNN learns to emphasize the edges in the encoder, to
predict crisp boundaries by an auxiliary edge supervision, and to fuse its
output with the original CNN output. We evaluate the effectiveness of the
EG-CNN with various mainstream CNNs on two publicly available datasets, BraTS
19 and KiTS 19 for brain tumor and kidney semantic segmentation. We demonstrate
how the addition of EG-CNN consistently improves segmentation accuracy and
generalization performance.
  We also conduct settlement analysis to show how EG-CNN learns to emphasize
edges. We find that the EG-CNN is able to increase the intensity of foreground
objects while preserving their original shape and boundary smoothness. This is
in contrast to previous methods that use multi-task learning with separate
edge and segmentation labels. We demonstrate that our model is able to reduce
over-segmentation (i.e., segmentation errors) by learning to emphasize boundary
shapes.

module can improve segmentation performance (lower DICE score gap) as the
anatomy of interest gets smaller (e.g., tumor size). This suggests that the
EG-CNN is more effective in scoring small structures. We also find that the
edge map learned by the EG-CNN can raise the segmentation accuracy on
infrequently labeled classes (e.g., the Blood Vessel class in BraTS19). The
source code is available at:

Biases in the dataset can be learned by the model and degrade the
generalizability of the applications. There are studies on debiased models.
However, scientists and practitioners are difficult to identify implicit biases
in the datasets, which causes lack of reliable unbias test datasets to valid
models. To tackle this issue, we first define the data intrinsic bias
attribute, and then propose a novel bias identification framework for medical
image datasets. The framework contains two major components, KlotskiNet and
Bias Discriminant Direction Analysis(bdda), where KlostkiNet is to build the
mapping which makes backgrounds to distinguish positive and negative samples
and bdda provides a theoretical solution on determining bias attributes.
Experimental results on three datasets show the effectiveness of the bias
attributes discovered by the framework.
  We also find that in some cases the models trained by us find similar
performance on the conventional test datasets, indicating the limited capability
of current debiased models on removing implicit biases, which highlights the
necessity of tackling biases from the dataset side.
  Finally, we believe that our framework provides a general solution for
identifying biases in image datasets, and could be applied to other areas.
Further work includes building more reliable debiased models and investigating
the generalization on other image datasets.
  The code is available at https://github.com/zwzhao123/BiasAnalysisForMedicalImageDatasets.

strategy (RL-DA) for adapting a pre-trained model to a real-world live data
feed setting while interacting with the environment and collecting continual
feedback. RL-DA is evaluated on SER tasks, including cross-corpus and
cross-language domain adaption schema. Evaluation results show that in a live
data feed setting, RL-DA outperforms a baseline strategy by 11% and 14% in
cross-corpus and cross-language scenarios, respectively.
  Which domain adaptation (DA) technique should be used in a specific scenario
to achieve the best performance? The success of different techniques can depend
on many factors, including the nature of the data and the set of source domains
available. However, current choices are often empirical and can be time
consuming to evaluate. In this paper, we propose a generic framework, called
CoDA (Combined Domain Adaptation), to combine the strengths of multiple DA
techniques, so that the model is trained in a way that leverages the best
features of each technique. More specifically, we use a mixture of experts (MoE)
to combine the outputs of different DA models, where the weights for each expert
are learned via a meta-learning objective. We evaluate our approach on three
common DA settings: (1) single-source multi-source, (2) multi-source multi-task,
and (3) semi-supervised single source. Evaluation results show that our approach
achieves better performances than baselines in all the settings above.
Furthermore, CoDA allows us to combine the strengths of different transfer
learning strategies, leading to superior performance gains.

evident change in the local structure at about 5.5 GPa indicating that the
evolution of the local structure under applied pressure seems to not follow
crystallographic changes (long range order). Nuclear forward scattering (NFS)
measurement reveal the development of magnetic ordering in BFTO at 5K with high
pressures. A progressive increase in magnetic order is observed with increase
in pressure at 5K. Further, NFS measurements carried out at constant pressure
(6.4GPa) and different temperatures indicate that the developed magnetism
disappears at 200K. The results suggest that application of high pressure
acts as a tool to tune property of BFTO.

derive a priori and localized error bounds for the flight time of discrete
paths relative to the optimal continuous trajectory, in terms of the graph
density and the given wind field. These bounds allow designing graphs with an
optimal local connectivity structure. The properties of the bounds are
illustrated on a set of benchmark problems. It turns out that localization
improves the error bound by four orders of magnitude, but still leaves ample

purpose we derive an error bound in terms of the wind field's Hessian, which

we investigate localization based on the discrete shortest path itself, which
yields excellent results for common graph densities, but is computationally
expensive. We also develop a simple localization strategy based on a rough
continuous estimation of the optimal trajectory. This also yields satisfactory
results for the given graph densities.

too sparse graph leads to a disregarded discretization error, while a too dense

lower connectivity for the long-range connections with negligible loss of

polynomials defined as Wronskians of classic Hermite polynomials appear in a
number of mathematical physics problems as well as in the theory of random
matrices and 1D SUSY quantum mechanics. Being quadratic at infinity, those

quantum non-singular potentials come as a dressing of the harmonic oscillator
by polynomial Heisenberg algebra ladder operators. To this end, all generalized

inequality between the degree of a polynomial and the number of its zeros, distanced

applicable to generalized Hermite polynomials and leads to the exact upper bound
of localized region, starting from the smallest degrees.

construct solutions of the discrete Schr\"odinger equation and, in particular,

show that the liquidity cost is a multiplication of the unit liquidity cost,

than buying options directly (i.e., writing an option rather than hedging it)
for sellers and less costly for buyers. This liquidity cost is a reason for
the price discrepancy between the two markets and can be accounted for in
pricing options using historical delta data.

a portfolio of options in different scenarios. This cost is shown to be
asymmetric and can be both heavily skewed to the right and heavy-tailed. This
means that despite a low average cost, a sellermanaging a large portfolio can
still experience very high liquidity costs. A fast-to-execute algorithm that
minimizes the liquidity cost is also provided. This algorithm is based on a
recursive formula and is capable of calculating the minimum liquidity cost to
hedge the next expiration option with a given delta. It can be used by a
sellermanaging a portfolio of options to significantly reduce their liquidity
cost. The use of this algorithm in a real-life scenario is also discussed.

significant bandwidth in the communication process. We propose a distributed
gradient-based optimization algorithm in which the non-malicious agents
exchange quantized information with one another. We prove convergence of the
solution to a neighborhood of the optimal solution, and characterize the
solutions obtained under the communication-constrained environment and presence
of malicious agents. Numerical simulations to illustrate the results are also
presented.

agents communicate continuously with each other. In Section V, we prove
convergence of the proposed algorithm when the non-malicious agents communicate
with each other discretely. Numerical simulations to illustrate the results are
presented in Section VI.

let alone why they help. We use BART as an instance and show its effectiveness
in the task. To explain why BART helps word ordering, we extend analysis with
probing and empirically identify that syntactic dependency knowledge in BART is

related partial tree linearization task, which readily extends our analysis.
## Beyond Models
We investigate factors of BART that are beneficial to the task. Among them,
we find that syntactic dependency knowledge in BART is the most reliable
explanation for its effectiveness in word ordering. We use a string-based
probing experiment to support this claim. In particular, we find that the
performance of BART in word ordering correlates with the quality of BART as a
machine translation model, which in turn correlates with its syntactic dependency
knowledge. We also rule out that other sources of information, such as
phonological knowledge, is the cause of BART's performance in word ordering.
## On Tasks
We study BART in two related constrained language generation tasks:
wordordering and partial tree linearization. In partial tree linearization,
agents place a subset of words to the beginning of the sentence while
respecting the word order. We use the standard data release policy of the
web-tree linearization shared task. BART improves over a strong baseline on
this task. Analysis on BART in partial tree linearization extends our
investigation of the model in word ordering, where we can also monitor the
performance as we constrain the output.
  Word ordering and partial tree linearization share much knowledge, including
syntactic dependency knowledge. We observe performance gains with BART in
partial tree linearization, suggesting that the model's effectiveness in
word ordering carries over to the larger task of linearization.

investigate constrained language generation tasks that require varying amounts
of contextualized prediction history. We find that BART's capability to use
contextualized knowledge agrees with its performance in these tasks: it
significantly outperforms a smaller transformer model on word ordering, but
only shows minor gains over a strong baseline in partial tree linearization.

robust min-max optimization problem, the learning problem can be reduced to a
modified robust minimization problem and solved efficiently. Leveraging the
newly formulated optimization problem, we propose a robust version of
Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD), coined Distributionally

because of the complexity of the systems involved, deriving a mathematical
model which can be used for clustering and community detection, is often
impossible. Moreover, while clustering dynamical systems, it is imperative that
the dynamical nature of the underlying system is taken into account. In this
paper, we propose a novel approach for clustering dynamical systems purely from
time-series data which inherently takes into account the dynamical evolution of
the underlying system. In particular, we define a \emph{distance/similarity}
measure between the states of the system which is a function of the influence
that the states have on each other, and use the proposed measure for clustering
of the dynamical system. For data-driven computation we leverage the Koopman
operator framework which takes into account the nonlinearities (if present) of
the underlying system, thus making the proposed framework applicable to a wide
range of application areas. We illustrate the efficacy of the proposed approach
by clustering three different dynamical systems, namely, a linear system, which
acts like a proof of concept, the highly non-linear IEEE 39 bus transmission
network and dynamic variables obtained from atmospheric data over the Amazon
region. A comparison with existing community detection measures like
Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM), K-Means, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and
Granger Causality is also presented to show the superiority of the proposed
approach.

fundamental role on dynamical processes evolving on heterogeneous networks.
These localization analyses are frequently grounded, for example, on
eigenvectors of adjacency or non-backtracking matrices which emerge in theories
of dynamic processes near to an active to inactive transition. We advance in
this problem gauging nodal activity to quantify the localization in dynamical
processes on networks whether they are near to a transition or not. The method
is generic and applicable to theory, stochastic simulations, and real data. We
investigate spreading processes on a wide spectrum of networks, both
analytically and numerically, showing that nodal activity can present complex
patterns depending on the network structure. Using annealed networks we show
that a localized state at the transition and an endemic phase just above it are
not incompatible features of a spreading process. We also report that epidemic
prevalence near to the transition is determined by the delocalized component of
the network even when the analysis of the inverse participation ratio indicates
a localized activity. Also, dynamical processes with distinct critical
exponents can be described by the same localization pattern. Turning to
quenched networks, a more complex picture, depending on the type of activation
and on the range of degree exponent, is observed and discussed. Our work paves
an important path for investigation of localized activity in spreading and
other processes on networks.
  Moreover, we map a spin-glass theory of opinion formation to a spreading
process, finding that the dynamical process captured is localized, which is
related to the fact that the opinion formation process has a sharp phase transition
in the thermodynamic limit. This localization differs from that of spreading
processes, which can be considered as a background for the opinion formation
dynamics.
  Finally, applying our methodology to the study of vaccination processes we
find that the localization of the endogenous activity in a network is related
to the efficacy of vaccination in eliminating a disease. More specifically, a
localized activity with a large fraction of active nodes is a necessary condition
for the existence of a threshold percentage of vaccination above which the disease
can be eliminated.
  In summary, a detailed analysis of localization in spreading and opinion
formation processes is presented, highlighting the complexity of the phenomenon
in different networks. Also, a method to investigate localization in dynamical
processes on complex networks is introduced, applicable to theory, simulations,
and data.

  We introduce Historical Form Recognition (HFR), a new task, to extract
information from historical forms. Historical forms are varied in layout and
have degraded images, yet effective extraction methods can improve overall
accuracy of historical document repositories and research centers. While
existing approaches to form recognition focus on modern forms, the harder domain
of historical forms has received little attention. We introduce HFR-200F, a
new dataset of 200 historical form images (late 1800s, early 1900s) with
manually transcribed text. HFR-200F covers varying form layouts and contains
difficult images due to noise, degradation, and partial occlusion. We also
introduce a set of challenging heuristic-based baselines, and report results
using state-of-the-art, template-free approaches. Our empirical evidence
suggests that current template-free approaches are near state-of-the-art on
HFR-200F, achieving greater than 90% word accuracy.

network (of unknown size) under the presence of a large number of Byzantine
nodes. We assume the full information model where the Byzantine nodes have
complete knowledge about the entire state of the network at every round
(including random choices made by all the nodes), have unbounded computational
power, and can deviate arbitrarily from the protocol.
  Our main contribution is a randomized distributed algorithm that estimates
the size of a network under the presence of a large number of Byzantine nodes.
In particular, our algorithm estimates the size of a sparse, "small-world",
expander network with up to $O(n^{1 - \delta})$ Byzantine nodes, where $n$ is
the (unknown) network size and $\delta$ can be be any arbitrarily small (but
fixed) positive constant. Our algorithm outputs a (fixed) constant factor
estimate of $\log(n)$ with high probability; the correct estimate of the
network size will be known to a large fraction ($(1 - \epsilon)$-fraction, for
any fixed positive constant $\epsilon$) of the honest nodes. Our algorithm is
fully distributed, lightweight, and simple to implement, runs in $O(\log^3{n})$
rounds, and requires nodes to send and receive messages of only small-sized
messages per round; any node's local computation cost per round is also small.
  Our algorithm relies on a new, simple-to-implement, lightweight, and randomized
protocol that ensures robustness to a large number of Byzantine nodes, which
avoids the use of cryptographic primitives, reliable memory, and global
leaders. The protocol does not assume any underlying cryptographic primitive,
rely on reliable memory to store state, or have a global leader, and ensures
that all honest nodes can calculate a robust estimate of the network size.
  We believe that our algorithm is relevant to many applications where the
network size is unknown and there is a large number of malicious nodes.
  Keywords: Distributed algorithms, robustness to Byzantine faults, sparse
networks, unknown network size, large number of malicious nodes, network
sampling, robust estimation.

protocol to estimate the network size from the sampled nodes. We extended this
protocol to remove the leader assumption, and the results still hold.

nonparametric short-term queue length estimation in terms of cycle-by-cycle
partially observed queues from probe vehicles. The method does not assume
random arrivals and does not assume any primary parameters or estimation of any

at the end of red signal phase) are represented by a Negative Hypergeometric
distribution. The estimators obtained are compared with parametric methods and
simple highway capacity manual methods using field test data involving probe
vehicles. The analysis indicates that the nonparametric methods presented in
this paper match the accuracy of parametric methods used in the field test data

methodology including data sources, tools, and techniques used to develop the
combinatorial methods. Section 3 presents the development of the nonparametric

results of the field tests. Section 6 provides a discussion of the results. And

  Traffic state estimation using probe vehicle data has been an active area of
research. Research in this area has been summarized in several survey papers
e.g., [1, 2]. Advanced parametric methods have been developed to estimate
queues using probe vehicle data. For example, [3, 4] have developed methods
using Gaussian mixture models. [5] developed a hamming distance method. [6]
developed a nonparametric method using Bayesian approach. Other methods have
been summarized in several survey papers e.g., [1, 2]. There is still a
need to develop methods that are simple to implement, do not require estimation
of parameters, and are robust to rare events. Simple methods have been
developed for estimating queues on highways. For example, [7] developed a
method to estimate queues on highways that does not require estimation of
parameters. However, these methods are not applicable to signalized intersections
where queues are affected by signal control. This paper presents methods for
estimating queues on signalized intersections that do not require estimation of

on the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless (CTT) decomposition, in which
instead of solving the Hamiltonian constraint as a 2nd order elliptic equation
for a choice of mean curvature $K$, we solve an algebraic equation for $K$ for
a choice of conformal factor. By doing so, we evade the existence and
uniqueness problem of solutions of the Hamiltonian constraint without using the
usual conformal rescaling of the source terms. This is particularly important
when the sources are fundamental fields, as reconstructing the fields'
configurations from the rescaled quantities is potentially problematic. Using
an iterative multigrid solver, we show that this method provides rapid
convergent solutions for several initial conditions that have not yet been
studied in numerical relativity; namely (i) periodic inhomogeneous spacetimes
with large random Gaussian scalar field perturbations and (ii) asymptotically
flat black hole spacetimes with rotating scalar clouds.

for the CTT decomposition. It is based on a new multigrid scheme using a
modified version of the FAS (Full Approximation Scheme) algorithm. This is
partially implemented in CUDA to obtain very efficient solutions of the
conformal equation and the conformally related momentum constraints on a
typical GPU. The gain in the timing for the case of asymptotically flat
black hole spacetimes with rotating scalar clouds is $\approx 5$.
  Finally, we show that there is no difference in the evolution of several
quantities (e.g. scalar field, spacetime curvature, conformal factor) whether
we solve the conformal equation for the mean curvature $K$ or the algebraic

  We propose a unified algorithm called Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE)
to tackle two key questions in knowledge distillation for ranking models. PILE
ensembles multi-teacher logits supervised by label information in an iterative
way and achieved competitive performance in both offline and online experiments.
The proposed method has been deployed in a real-world commercial search system.
Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/yuanyuyuan/PILE.
  From a theoretical perspective, we give a discussion on the convergence of
the iteration in PILE. The iteration in PILE is an expectation maximization
process and it is convergent at least locally. We also prove that the local
convergence rate of the iteration is geometerically convergent under some
conditions. From a practical perspective, we evaluate the performance of a
ranking system using three knowledge distillation models: PILE, Logits
Ensemble, and Temporal Ensemble Distillation. We give a discussion on the
advantages and disadvantages of each model based on our experiments.

that the teachers in PILE are all self-built models. We can further extend the
teachers in PILE to include both self-built models and commercial ones and
evaluate their effects on ranking systems.

beam dynamics as well as
the most relevant beam loss mechanisms in circular machines will be presented
in this lecture. This lecture is intended for physicists and engineers with
little or no knowledge of this subject.
  A detailed discussion of the relevant equations governing transverse and
longitudinal beam dynamics, including a discussion of possible dynamical
instabilities, will be presented. An introduction to the tools used for the
design and analysis of beam dynamics issues, such as Russell, MAD and
Twiss-analysis, will also be presented.
  A discussion of the different types of beam loss mechanisms will be
presented, such as, beam-loss mechanisms induced by the beam-surrounding-vacuum
system, electrical-discharge-related losses, and radiative-related losses. In
addition, an introduction to the tools used for the analysis of electromagnetic
fields and material properties, such as COMSOL and reflectivity-measurements,
will be presented.
  Finally, measures that can be implemented to minimize beam losses will be
presented.

non-autonomous obstacle problems of the form
  \begin{equation*}
  \min \left\{\int_{\Omega}f\left(x, Dv(x)\right)dx\,:\, v\in
  \mathcal{K}_\psi(\Omega)\right\},
  \end{equation*} where the function $f$ satisfies $p-$growth conditions with
respect to the gradient variable, for $1<p<2$, and $\mathcal{K}_\psi(\Omega)$
is the class of admissible functions. Here we show that, if the obstacle $\psi$
is bounded, then a Sobolev regularity assumption on the gradient of the
obstacle $\psi$ transfers to the gradient of the solution, provided the partial
map $x\mapsto D_\xi f(x,\xi)$ belongs to a Sobolev space, $W^{1, p+2}$. The
novelty here is that we deal with subquadratic growth conditions with respect
to the gradient variable, i.e. $f(x, \xi)\approx a(x)|\xi|^p$ with $1<p<2,$ and
where the map $a$ belongs to a Sobolev space.
  We propose different approaches to handle this problem. The first one is based
on a suitable representation formula of the solution which allows to apply
differentiability results for integral functionals with non smooth data. The
second one is based on a representation of the solution as a continuous selection
of the smallest subgradient of the obstacle from the perspective of the
potential theory for Sobolev spaces. The third one is based on a new approach
which combines higher differentiability, representation formulas and gradient
regularity of obstacles.
  Finally, we apply our results to prove the existence of strong solutions to
non-homogeneous obstacle problems of p-Laplace type.

catastrophic failure of QA, whereas a certain decoherence process can be used
to avoid such failure. More specifically, when we include anti-ferromagnetic
interactions (i.e., typical non-stoquastic terms) in the Hamiltonian, we are
unable to prepare the target ground state even with an infinitely long

that, when we add a certain type of decoherence, we can obtain the ground state
after QA for these cases. This is because, even when symmetry exists, the
addition of decoherence breaks the symmetry. Moreover, the use of decoherence
can avoid the crossing of energy levels during QA. We also show that another
type of decoherence can lead to a complete failure of the ground-state search.
Thus, it is necessary to investigate how decoherence affects QA in general.
Additionally, our results show that the efficiency of QA depends on the choice
of the problem Hamiltonian.

In contrast, different types of neural networks may specialize in learning different types of task relationships. From this perspective, we propose the Co-Net model for multi-task learning, which consists of multiple modules with different types of neural networks to learn multiple tasks with diverse task relationships. ofiller-modified polymer matrices have
immense potential to improve the safety of high-risk engineering structures.
These materials are intrinsically self-sensing because their electrical
conductivity is affected by deformations and damage. This property, known as
piezoresistivity, has been extensively leveraged for conductivity-based damage
detection via electrical resistance change methods and tomographic imaging
techniques such as electrical impedance tomography (EIT). Although these
techniques are very effective at detecting the presence of damage, they suffer
from an inability to provide precise information about damage shape, size, or
mechanism. This is particularly detrimental for laminated composites which can
suffer from complex failure modes, such as delaminations, that are difficult to
detect. To that end, we herein propose a new technique for precisely
determining damage shape and size in self-sensing composites. Our technique
makes use of a genetic algorithm (GA) integrated with realistic physics-based
damage models to recover precise damage shape from conductivity changes imaged
via EIT. We experimentally validate this technique on carbon nanofiber
(CNF)-modified glass fiber-reinforced polymer (GFRP) laminates by considering
two specific damage mechanisms: through-holes and delaminations. Our results
show that this novel technique can accurately reconstruct multiple
through-holes with radii as small as 1.5 mm and depths up to 10 mm, as well as
a single delamination with a width of 1.8 cm and depth up to 6 mm. The use of
GA to search for the optimal damage shape and size allows our technique to
accurately capture complex damage shapes and yield precise spatial
information. The GA searched damage space is shown to be merely seconds long,
making this technique capable of real-time damage reconstruction on a
microsecond timescale. Furthermore, we show that CNF content can improve the
ability to detect delaminations, while also reducing conductivity. While this
technique was specifically developed for laminated composites, it can be
applied to any composite system, provided that the conductivity changes due to
damage are noticeable.

such performance by effectively leveraging various forms of side information on

More precisely, the algorithm approximately solves an optimal control problem
encoding the system's desired behavior. To this end, it constructs and

the approximate solution with respect to the optimal control with known

F-16 aircraft simulator and MuJoCo's environments illustrate that, despite the
scarcity of data, the algorithm can provide performance comparable to
reinforcement learning algorithms trained over millions of environment
interactions. Besides, we show that the algorithm outperforms existing
techniques combining system identification and model predictive control.

system failure, and the algorithm must reconstruct the failure from the data
recorded before the termination. Here, too, the algorithm is able to produce a

students' ability to keep up with the pace of instruction in a university level
physics course, with a focus on the heterogeneous impact of remote learning on
different demographic groups. Student learning data is collected from 70 online
learning modules assigned as both online homework and self-study material in
both Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters, with the first 41 modules being
assigned before campus closure in Spring 2020. Students' ability to stay on
track is measured by three data indicators: percentage of modules submitted
before the due date, percentage of modules submitted early for extra credit,
and percentage of modules properly engaged with. The student population is
divided into two demographic groups according to each of the four demographic
variables: Gender, Ethnicity, Transfer Status and First generation status. All
three data indicators from both semesters are first compared between each pair
of demographic groups within the same semester, and then compared within the
same group between the two semesters. Exam and course scores are also compared
between demographics groups in Fall 2020 and against scores from the Fall 2019
semester. The analysis revealed that remote learning significantly reduced
on-time and early submission for first-generation students, but increased the
frequency of early submission for transfer students. Under-represented minority
students had higher percentage of engaged modules during the pandemic, while
non-URM students had a sharper decrease. There was no significant change in any
indicator for both gender and transfer status groups. Temporary submission
delay was common after campus closure, but only for non-first-generation
students. Results from Fall 2020 compare to those from Fall 2019 reveal that
examination and course scores for students with different demographic traits
varied significantly, underlining the need for effective instructional
interventions to close score gaps in this course.

BCIs to elementary gait tasks, such as the initiation and termination of
walking. To restore more complex gait functions, BCIs must accurately decode
additional degrees of freedom from brain signals. In this study, we used
subdurally recorded electrocorticogram (ECoG) signals from able-bodied subjects
to design a decoder capable of predicting the walking state and step rate
information. We recorded ECoG signals from the motor cortices of two
individuals as they walked on a treadmill at different speeds. Our offline
analysis demonstrated that the state information could be decoded from >16
minutes of ECoG data with an unprecedented accuracy of 99.8%. Additionally,
using a Bayesian filter approach, we achieved an average correlation
coefficient between the decoded and true step rates of 0.934. When combined,
these decoders may yield decoding accuracies sufficient to safely operate
present-day walking prostheses.

be used to quantify uncertainty and relevance. However, in practice, it can be
difficult to compute these quantities for arbitrary probability distributions,
particularly if the probability mass functions or densities cannot be
evaluated. This paper introduces a computational approach, based on Nested
Sampling, to evaluate entropies of probability distributions that can only be
sampled. I demonstrate the method on three examples: a simple gaussian example
where the key quantities are available analytically; (ii) an experimental
design example about scheduling observations in order to measure the period of
an oscillating signal; and (iii) predicting the future from the past in a
heavy-tailed scenario.
  Nested Sampling is a method for modelling a wide range of physical
phenomena, from the behaviour of matter at the highest energies that can be
achieved in laboratories on Earth, to the evolution of the whole Universe
itself. Yet despite its widespread application, including in some astrophysical
works that consider entropy (e.g. Wheeler et al. 2000; Turner 2002), the
algorithm is generally used as an 'inside trick' of the nested sampling code,
rather than being made available as a'standalone' sample-based method for
calculating these entropies. This is probably because, in practice, it requires
an extra level of technical assistance, as it requires users to implement some
of the components of the algorithm themselves. To make it more widely available
for these purposes, I present a new algorithm, based on nested sampling, to
compute these quantities. The new method is presented in Section 2, and then
demonstrated in Section 3 on the three examples mentioned above.
  In Section 4 I discuss the results, and present future directions in Section
5.

networks (GNNs) have been successfully used to learn data representations and
structures to solve classification and link prediction problems. The
applications of such methods are vast and diverse, but most of the current work
relies on the assumption of a static graph. This assumption does not hold for
many highly dynamic systems, where the underlying connectivity structure is
non-stationary and is mostly unobserved. Using a static model in these
situations may result in sub-optimal performance. In contrast, modeling changes
in graph structure with time can provide information about the system whose
applications go beyond classification. Most work of this type does not learn
effective connectivity and focuses on cross-correlation between nodes to
generate undirected graphs. An undirected graph is unable to capture direction
of an interaction which is vital in many fields, including neuroscience. To
bridge this gap, we developed dynamic effective connectivity estimation via
neural network training (DECENNT), a novel model to learn an interpretable
directed and dynamic graph induced by the downstream classification/prediction
task. DECENNT outperforms state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods on five different
tasks and infers interpretable task-specific dynamic graphs. The dynamic graphs
inferred from functional neuroimaging data align well with the existing
literature and provide additional information. Additionally, the temporal
connectivity maps inferred from neuroimaging data of people with schizophrenia
differ from those of healthy individuals, reflecting the semi-structural
abnormalities in connectivity of people with schizophrenia. In conclusion, DECENNT
is a novel model for estimating directed dynamic graphs that can be applied to
a variety of domains and data types.

differentiate the solution map of a (continuous) parametrized optimization
problem, opening up the possibility of embedding mathematical optimization
problems into end-to-end learnable models. These differentiability results can
lead to significant memory savings by providing an expression for computing the
derivative without needing to unroll the steps of the forward-pass optimization
procedure during the backward pass. However, the results typically require
inverting a large Hessian matrix, which is computationally expensive when
implemented naively. In this work we study two applications of deep declarative
networks -- robust vector pooling and optimal transport -- and show how problem
structure can be exploited to obtain very efficient backward pass computations
in terms of both time and memory. Our ideas can be used as a guide for
improving the computational performance of other novel deep declarative nodes.
We also provide a generic technique for splitting large HHessian matrices into
smaller ones, making our approach applicable to a wider range of problems. We
experimentally verify our findings, showing that these simple tricks can lead
to orders of magnitude improvements in backward pass performance.

show how it can be used to learn meaningful metric learning tasks. Our approach
can also be used to continue-training (learn from data) existing metric
learning solutions, leading to improvements in classification accuracy and
sensitivity to missing data.

solutions to integer programming problems, leading to a new approach to learning
with integer constraints. We experimentally verify that our approach is
comparable to (and sometimes superior to) existing algorithms for solving
integer programming problems.

declarative nodes are found useful by the community, and help to accelerate

the surface code,
currently provide the most feasible roadmap towards large-scale fault-tolerant
quantum computation. As such, obtaining fast and flexible decoding algorithms
for these codes, within the experimentally relevant context of faulty syndrome
measurements, is of critical importance. In this work, we show that the problem
of decoding such codes, in the full fault-tolerant setting, can be naturally
reformulated as a process of repeated interactions between a decoding agent and
a code environment, to which the machinery of reinforcement learning can be
applied to obtain decoding agents. As a demonstration, by using deepQ learning,
we obtain fast decoding agents for the surface code, for a variety of
noise-models.
  We find that for the commonly studied batch noise models, these learning
process is not needed as we can obtain closed form decoding rules that
outperform the established algorithms. Furthermore, we show that the learned
decoding rules can be naturally enhanced to be adaptive, to respond to
code-dependent noise patterns that may be encountered during the computation.
Finally, we show that these enhancing adaptations can be avoided by using another
learning strategy, to obtain decoders that are also compatible with continuous
noise processes.
  As we move towards implementing such decoders in actual experiments, it is
important to consider their cognitive and reliability properties. First, we show
that they possess a level of cognitive complexity which is comparable to that of
higher insects. Next, we demonstrate that we can simplify their structure, to
obtain simpler decoders which come accompanied with a decrease in noise-tolerance
but an increase in comprehensibility. Finally, we show that these decoders can
be trained to respond to an array of error types, to serve as versatile
components of hybrid error correction schemes.
  Overall, our work presents a comprehensive framework for addressing the
problem of fault-tolerant decoding, and highlights the benefits and drawbacks
of using learning in this context.
We argue that with minimal additional effort, a set of robust surface code
decoding algorithms, adaptable to different noise models, can be provided to
the community, to be used as a starting point for further development.
Finally, we emphasize that the framework itself is not specific to the surface
code, and can be applied to the study and development of decoding algorithms for
any other fault-tolerant code.

challenging. An alternative approach is quantum jump metrology [L. A. Clark

by continuously monitoring an open quantum system, while inducing
phase-dependent temporal correlations with the help of quantum feedback. Taking
this approach here, we analyse measurements of a relative phase in an optical
network of two cavities with quantum feedback in the form of laser pulses. It
is shown that the proposed approach can exceed the standard quantum limit
without the need for complex quantum states while being scalable and more
practical than previous related schemes.

subject to quantum jumps and quantum feedback, and we identify the optimum
feedback strategy by which the phase uncertainty can be minimized. We show how
the proposed approach can be implemented with an optical quantum memory and find
that it can outperform classical phase estimation schemes, such as radar. The
proposed method could also be applicable to other systems and in different
scenarios.

understood in terms of a classical limit of the quantum system's temporal
correlations, and the maximum precision achievable is given by the square of the
phased-coherent amplitude of the system. The partial summation of the
feedback process also leads to a enhancement of the metrological performance.
This is demonstrated through a bias correction term in the uncertainty analysis
and is shown to be applicable to a wide range of situations.

monitoring and feedback system. We discuss the reliable storage of feedback
information and the enhancement of the phase uncertainty reduction through the

performance and cost both at small and large scale.

specific (peripheral) patterns of communication that should be optimized
differently than the central patterns that have been widely studied. While
central patterns have high bandwidth and low latency, peripherals may have
significant latency and loss rates. We represent the overall network
performance as a network distance weight matrix and use graph algorithms to
simulate network performance at a larger scale. Finally, we show that our
network analysis and simulation can be directly integrated with HPC scaling
studies to give a complete picture of the system, factoring out the
consideration of network performance.

premise HPC systems for the workloads studied, although the difference in
performance is primarily due to the different OS and transport protocols. In

limit), the performance is similar to on-premise HPC systems. If we consider
central patterns and also the cost, cloud systems offer significant benefits
over on-premise HPC systems.

network theory, this work studies the extremal gain of optimal power control
over binary (on/off) power control, especially in large interference networks,
in search of new theoretical insights. Whereas numerical studies have already
established that in most practical settings binary power control is close to
optimal, the extremal analysis shows not only that there exist settings where
the gain from optimal power control can be quite significant, but also bounds
the extremal values of such gains from a GDoF perspective. As its main
contribution, this work explicitly characterizes the extremal GDoF gain of
optimal over binary power control as $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ for all $K$.
In particular, the extremal gain is bounded between $\lfloor \sqrt{K}\rfloor$
and $2.5\sqrt{K}$ for every $K$. For $K=2,3,4,5,6$ users, the precise extremal
gain is found to be $1, 3/2, 2, 9/4$ and $41/16$, respectively. Networks shown
to achieve the extremal gain may be interpreted as multi-tier heterogeneous
networks. It is worthwhile to note that because of their focus on asymptotic
analysis, the sharp characterizations of extremal gains are valuable primarily
to practitioners of extremal network theory and those interested in
non-asymptotic analysis.
  We also find it useful to illustrate two levers that can be employed to
customize extremal network theory towards the study of interference networks.
First, by specifying a network structure as the "target network", one can
study whether a given setting leads to a gain (loss) of power control over
binary power control by comparing the received signals of users in the target
network under these two power control schemes. This is in contrast to
extremal network theory which studies such a gain (loss) by finding two
distinct networks. The second lever allows us to study specific discrete
settings by analyzing the smallest difference between largest and smallest
sum-interference in discrete settings. We find that for some discrete settings
of interest, the smallest such difference is smaller than previously known, thus
leading to a smaller gain (loss) of power control over binary power control. A
brief discussion of binary power control in multi-user Multiple-Input Multiple-Output
(MIMO) networks is also provided

is a challenging and open
robo-physics problem since the uncertainty in terrain dynamics introduced by
ground deformation complicates the dynamical modelling and control methods.
Moreover, learning how (e.g. what controls and mechanisms) to move efficiently
and stably on soft ground is a bigger issue. This work seeks to control a 1D
monopod hopper to jump to desired height. To achieve this goal, I first set up
and validate a discrete element method (DEM) based soft ground simulation
environment of a spherical granular material. With this simulation environment,
I generate resistive force theory (RFT) based models of the ground reaction
force. Then I use the RFT model to develop a feedforward force control for this
robot. In the DEM simulation, I use feedback control to compensate for
variations in the ground reaction force from the RFT model predictions. With
the feedback control, the robot tracks the desired trajectories well and
reaches the desired height after five hops. It reduces the apex position errors
a lot more than a pure feedforward control. I also change the area of the
robots square foot from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2. The feedback controller is able to
deal with the ground reaction force fluctuations even when the foot dimensions
are on the order of a grain diameter.
  From an industrial perspective, developing an off the shelf
motion-planning-library would be super useful. It could be based on some form
of sampling based methods, e.g. bidirectional helical search, or centralized
planning using dynamical models and optimal control methods. Either way, it
would be super useful to have a high level language, say in python, where you
can easily plan and customize locomotion trajectories for your robot.
  In this work, I develop a python based locomotion planning library,
'fastfoot'. It uses inverse kinematics to ensure generic compatibility with
serial legged robots. It contains 3 main modules, 'foot', 'body' and 'chain'.
'foot' contains the base classes and functions for feet. 'body' contains the
base classes and functions for the body of the robot e.g. helical upright,
inverted pendulum. 'chain' contains functions for actuated chains e.g.
brackets, scissor mechanisms. It also contains a set of high level functions to
plan locomotion for some well known robots e.g. Insect, Dinosaur, Trackbot.

contact interaction model is revisited in this manuscript. The dressed masses

  In the study of meson elastic form factors, the interaction in the momentum
space is usually treated by means of Lévy-like form factors introduced
phenomenologically. The corresponding parameters are often determined by the
data so that the calculated form factors are in fact an fit to the data. In
this manuscript, we go beyond this framework by treating the momentum space
interaction explicitly as a contact interaction for the purpose of obtaining
the elastic form factors and charge radii for several mesons.
  For the pseudoscalar mesons such as $\pi$, $\eta$ and $\eta'$, the charge
radii obtained here are consistent with the perturbative QCD predictions. For
the scalar mesons $f_0(500)$ and $k_0^*(1430)$, the charge radii are also
reasonable and relevant to the discussion of the structure of these mesons.
For the axial-vector mesons $\rho$, $\omega$ and $\phi$, the charge radii are
also reasonable and relevant to the discussion of the structure of these mesons.
In particular, the charge radius of $\rho$ is sensitive to the diquark mass
which is determined by the contact interaction in the quark antiquark sector.
  In general, the charge radii of mesons are sensitive to the quark masses.
For the mesons formed of two identical quarks, the charge radii are also
influenced by the diquark mass if it is a constituent quark system. For the
mesons formed of two differently flavored quarks, the influence of the diquark
mass to the charge radii is negligible.

without negation. All human languages have some form of negation. Despite this,
negation remains a challenging phenomenon for current natural language
understanding systems. To facilitate the future development of models that can
process negation effectively, we present CONDAQA, the first English reading
comprehension dataset which requires reasoning about the implications of
negated statements in paragraphs. We collect paragraphs with diverse negation
cues, then have crowdworkers ask questions about the implications of the
negated statement in the passage. We also have workers make three kinds of
edits to the passage -- paraphrasing the negated statement, changing the scope
of the negation, and reversing the negation -- resulting in clusters of
question-answer pairs that are difficult for models to answer with spurious
shortcuts. CONDAQA features 14,182 question-answer pairs with over 200 unique
negation cues and is challenging for current state-of-the-art models. The best
performing model on CONDAQA (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) achieves only 42% on our
consistency metric, well below human performance which is 81%. We release our
dataset, along with fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot evaluations, to
facilitate the development of future NLP methods that work on negated language.
This work is based on a thesis chapter that appeared in the thesis of A
Goyal. We use the acronym CONDAQA to refer to both the dataset and the thesis.
A version of this work with additional analysis and results appears in Goyal
et al. (2022).

evaluates them using real-life event data.
  Given a complete alignment for a trace, we define infix/postfix alignments
as the parts of the complete alignment, propose approaches to computing them,
and evaluate them using real-life event data from the airline industry. Our
approaches are implemented in a tool available at
https://github.com/eplanet/ixfy-tools.
  The approaches are evaluated using alignability, accuracy, and performance as
criteria. We find that prefix alignments can be used to compute infix
alignments and that different distance measures are suitable for different
settings. Furthermore, we propose a method to visualize infix/postfix
alignments, which facilitates the comparison of alignments on event logs and
supports the detection of process issues. The proposed method is evaluated on
a set of benchmarks and is shown to have good performance.

velocity is expected to approach the conformal limit ($c_s/c=1/\sqrt{3}$) at
high densities and should also fulfill the causality limit ($c_s/c<1$).

that the sound velocity of dense matter could be an important indicator for a
deconfinement phase transition, where a particular shape might be expected for
its density dependence. In this work, we explore the general properties of the
sound velocity and the adiabatic index of dense matter in hybrid stars, as well
as in neutron stars and quark stars. Various conditions are employed for
hadron-quark phase transition with varying interface tension. We find that the
expected behavior of the sound velocity can also be achieved by the
nonperturbative properties of the quark phase, in addition to a deconfinement
phase transition. And it leads to a more compact star with a similar mass. We
then propose a new class of quark star equation of states, which could be
tested by future high-precision radius measurements of pulsar-like objects.
These new quark star equations of states are also compatible with the
condition of high-density energy density polytrope.

rotating star properties, including the maximum spin limit, the mass--radius
relation, and the sequence of different rotation modes. By comparing the
non-rotating and rotating properties of quark stars with those of neutron
stars, we can further constrain the unknown quark matter equation of state.

and $T_2(V_2, E_2)$ defines a one-to-one mapping between nodes in $T_1$ and
$T_2$ that preserves ancestor relationship. For unordered trees the problem of
finding a maximum-weight Tai mapping is known to be NP-complete. In this work,
we define an anti Tai mapping $M\subseteq V_1\times V_2$ as a binary relation
between two unordered labeled trees such that any two $(x,y), (x', y')\in M$
violate ancestor relationship and thus cannot be part of the same Tai mapping,
i.e. $(x\le x' \iff y\not \le y') \vee (x'\le x \iff y'\not \le y)$, given an
ancestor order $x<x'$ meaning that $x$ is an ancestor of $x'$. Finding a
maximum-weight anti Tai mapping arises in the cutting plane method for solving
the maximum-weight Tai mapping problem via integer programming. We give an
efficient polynomial-time algorithm for finding a maximum-weight anti Tai
mapping for the case when one of the two trees is a path and further show how
to extend this result in order to provide a polynomially computable lower bound
on the optimal anti Tai mapping for two unordered labeled trees. The latter
gives a significant improvement over the currently known pseudo polynomial
algorithm for that problem.
  We also investigate how anti Tai mappings are utilized in other problems. We
show that they are necessary in order to solve the minimum number of rotations
needed to transform one unordered labeled tree into another via a sequence of
rotations. We further show that they are useful in an algorithm for computing
the Buber-Webber distance between two unordered labeled trees.
  In conclusion, we suggest viewing anti Tai mappings as utility objects in
their own right rather than simply as tools for solving other problems.
Furthermore, we believe that the connection between anti Tai mappings and the
Buber-Webber distance is interesting and may lead to a better understanding of

performed numerical simulations to check the theoretical predictions. A

Sun, and the PPN $\gamma$ uncertainty. Numerical simulations of the astrometric

many other important rings and fields, the problem is still widely open. In
this paper, we present an explicit algorithm for decomposing an element of an
arbitrary global field (either a number field or a global function field) into
a sum of squares of minimal length.
  From a theoretical point of view, this is achieved by reducing the problem to
the one for the rings of integers (in the case of a number field) or polynomial
rings over a finite field (in the case of a global function field). For these
rings, we review and refine existing techniques to make them fully automated and
capable of handling very large inputs. We also introduce a uniform
implementation of these algorithms, together with a set of tools and techniques
that can be used to solve various related problems (like solving a system of
diophantine inequalities or computing an optimal Hermite normal form).
  We also report on a computer algebra system, developed by the first author, that
informs this paper. This system is capable of solving very large examples in
fields of several variables, and sometimes its answers were used to guide our
theoretical developments. We illustrate its capabilities by solving several
problems that were previously unsolved (because of their large size). The
implementation of this system, together with the theoretical results
presented in this paper, form the basis of a fully automated algorithm for
decomposing an element of a global field into a sum of squares of minimal
length.

capable of improving the existing partial results towards the 16th problem on
Millennium Prize Problems: given a polynomial $F(x_1,\dots,x_k)$ with which we
can control most of its irreducible factors, how many such factors does it
usually have?

polypharmacy side effect identification, drug-drug interaction prediction and

theoretical view of relational machine learning models which can address these
tasks. We provide fundamental definitions, compare existing model architectures

  Relational machine learning models for drug data analysis often handle
high-dimensional input representations and output a large number of possible
interactions or side effects. These interactions and side effects can have
complex structures and may be difficult to visualize. Therefore, interpreting
and understanding the predictions of such models is crucial. We define
different types of output interpretations such as rule-based methods, 1-line
descriptions and hierarchical classifications, and review existing methods which
attempt to explain predictions of relational machine learning models. We
emphasize recent attempts to create generic explanation methods which are not
domain specific, and we discuss future research directions in this area.

prediction in various domains, including social networks, chemistry and
pharmacology. Here, we study imputation of sensitive information from graph
data using GNNs. We create a new dataset covering some aspect of real life and
investigate how different GNN models learn to impute identity from a
corresponding social graph. We show that GNNs are capable of learning to impute
identity from graph data and the predictions of GNNs are sensitive to privacy
settings. We also discuss social implications of the findings and possible

likelihood that offenders return to the criminal justice system in the future.

benefit analysis suggests that the treatment-induced decrease in future crime
would be more than sufficient to offset the costs of providing treatment.

which one fundamental challenge is to understand the influence of data quality
to ML training -- "Which training examples are 'guilty' in making the trained
ML model predictions inaccurate or unfair?" Modeling data influence for ML
training has attracted intensive interest over the last decade, and one popular
framework is to compute the Shapley value of each training example with respect
to utilities such as validation accuracy and fairness of the trained ML model.
Unfortunately, despite recent intensive interest and research, existing methods
only consider a single ML model "in isolation" and do not consider an
end-to-end ML pipeline that consists of data transformations, feature
extractors, and ML training.
  We present DataScope (ease.ml/datascope), the first system that efficiently
computes Shapley values of training examples over an end-to-end ML pipeline,
and illustrate its applications in data debugging for ML training. To this end,
we first develop a novel algorithmic framework that computes Shapley value over
a specific family of ML pipelines that we call canonical pipelines: a positive
relational algebra query followed by a K-nearest-neighbor (KNN) classifier. We
show that, for many subfamilies of canonical pipelines, computing Shapley value
is in PTIME, contrasting the exponential complexity of computing Shapley value
in general. We then put this to practice -- given an sklearn dataset and a
relation algebra language, DataScope computes the Shapley value of each training
example over the final model prediction which is the result of composing all
relational queries and the KNN classifier. We also introduce a simple programming
api that allows users to compose DataScope with other tools in a pipeline, and
illustrate its effectiveness with several examples.

issue, we first establish a theoretical framework to characterize this issue's
implications and worst-case scenarios. The analysis motivates our formulation
of the new task, supervised hypergraph reconstruction: reconstructing a
real-world hypergraph from its projected graph, with the help of some existing
knowledge of the application domain.
  To reconstruct hypergraph data, we start by analyzing hyperedge distributions
in the projection, based on which we create a framework containing two modules:
(1) to handle the enormous search space of potential hyperedges, we design a
sampling strategy with efficacy guarantees that significantly narrows the space
to a smaller set of candidates; (2) to identify hyperedges from the candidates,
we further design a hyperedge classifier in two well-working variants that
capture structural features in the projection. Extensive experiments validate
our claims, approach, and extensions. Remarkably, our approach outperforms all
baselines by an order of magnitude in accuracy on hard datasets. Our code and
data can be downloaded from bit.ly/SHyRe.
  Hypergraph reconstruction has a few potential impacts. First, it can address
the issue of incomplete hypergraph data. Second, it can evaluate the current
handling of missing data in graph mining, identifying the need for more research
along this direction. Third, it can analyze the limitations of current hypergraph
models and learn more appropriate higher-order data structures.
  Finally, hypergraph reconstruction brings hypergraph learning one step further
in terms of the emphasis on soundful task formulations, appropriate benchmark
data, and effective approaches that reflect on the specific characteristics of
hypergraph data.

multi-agent policies from pre-collected datasets, which is an important step
toward the deployment of multi-agent systems in real-world applications.
However, in practice, each individual behavior policy that generates
multi-agent joint trajectories usually has a different level of how well it
performs. e.g., an agent is a random policy while other agents are medium
policies. In the cooperative game with global reward, one agent learned by
existing offline MARL often inherits this random policy, jeopardizing the
performance of the entire team. In this paper, we investigate offline MARL with
explicit consideration on the diversity of agent-wise trajectories and propose
a novel framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) to address this
problem. Specifically, an attention-based reward decomposition network assigns
the credit to each agent through a differentiable key-value memory mechanism in
an offline manner. These decomposed credits are then used to reconstruct the
joint offline datasets into prioritized experience replay with individual
trajectories, thereafter agents can share their good trajectories and
conservatively train their policies with a graph attention network (GAT) based
critic. We evaluate our method in both discrete control (i.e., StarCraft II and
multi-agent particle environment) and continuous control (i.e, multi-agent
mujoco). The results indicate that our method achieves significantly better
results in complex and mixed offline MARL scenarios.

Neural Network. Most of the traditional image registration method
intensity-based, which use optimization algorithms to maximize the similarity
between to images. Although these methods can achieve good results for
kilovoltage images, the same does not occur for megavoltage images due to the
lower image quality. Also, these methods most of the times do not present a
good capture range. To deal with this problem, we propose the use of
Convolutional Neural Network. The experiments were performed using a dataset of
50 brain images. The results showed to be promising compared to traditional
image registration methods.
  We also presented an extension to this work, where the dataset used to train
the network does not contain brain images. The results showed to be promising
also for brain images, even not being trained with this specific data.
  Furthermore, the present work is related to the precision and the robustness
of the registration for brain tumors. The results showed to be promising for
different types of tumors.
  Finally, we presented a review about image registration methods for head
and neck cancer treatment. The present work surveyed intensity-based and
segmentation-based image registration methods. The extraction and the
reconstruction of the tumor volume from pre and intra treatment images is a
critical step in radiation therapy. In this context, the image registration
methods can help the medical staff to improve the treatment accuracy and
comfort of the patient. However, there is no works that present a survey about
this topic. Thus, we present a survey describing intensity-based and
segmentation-based image registration methods and their parameters.
  In conclusion, the present work reviews and presents different image
registration methods for radiotherapy.

the primary intention of showing the incompleteness of quantum mechanics; to
prove it, he uses the instantaneous nonlocal effects caused by the collapse of

Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism over the incompleteness of quantum mechanics.
Here, by using the Stern-Gerlach experiment (SGE), we demonstrate how the
instantaneous nonlocal feature of the collapse of the wave function together
with the single-particle entanglement can be used to produce the nonlocal
effect of steering. In the steering process Bob gets a quantum state depending
on which observable Alice decides to measure. To accomplish this, we fully
exploit the spreading (over large distances) of the entangled wave function of
the single-particle. In particular, we demonstrate that the nonlocality of the
single-particle entanglement allows the particle to know which detector Alice
is using to steer Bob's state. Therefore, notwithstanding strong
counterarguments, we prove that the single-particle entanglement gives rise to
truly nonlocal effects at two far a away places. This open the possibility of
using the single-particle entanglement for implementing truly nonlocal task.

allows Alice to transmit information to Bob's state. This is possible due to the
instantaneous nonlocal effect caused by the collapse of the wave function as
proposed by Einstein. Therefore, we prove that even in the single-particle
scenario Einstein's proposal leads to true nonlocal effects at two far a way
places. It is worthwhile to mention that this kind of nonlocality and the
corresponding steering task are impossible to be accomplished by classical
means. Therefore, the classical counterarguments over the incompleteness of the
quantum theory must be re-examined. It would be fascinating to see if this
single-particle nonlocality could be used to improve some classical communication
protocols.

the primary source of error is assumed to be spontaneous photon scattering. We
show that a five-qubit M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gate offers an approximately
$40\%$ improvement over two-qubit gates in terms of the fault tolerance
threshold. This result indicates an advantage of using multi-qubit gates in the

complex parities among QEC codes that is still "stabilizable" with local
operations. As such, it provides a natural benchmark to investigate the
optimality of any QEC scheme with respect to fault tolerance. Here, we study
the toric code subjected to spontaneous photon scattering errors, assuming that
the necessary controls are implemented via Raman transitions. Under these
assumptions, we derive a necessary and sufficient condition for fault tolerance
that the code can sustain before decoding. This condition is a function of the
quantum error rate, the temporal complexity of the parity checks, and the

using any particular method of implementing the toric code circuits. To
illustrate the necessary condition, we show that a toric code constructed from

10^{6}\ \rm M_{\odot}$) NSCs formed at high redshifts ($z\gtrsim 4$) can
increase the MRD by a factor of 2.5. Pop III binaries in globular clusters have

exhibits explosive growth during the last century. Despite the frequent use of
many tangible measures, such as citation, impact factor and g-index, to
quantify the influence of papers from different perspectives based on
scientific productivity, it has not yet been well understood how the
relationship between scientific productivity and knowledge amount turns out to
be, i.e., how the knowledge value of papers and knowledge amount vary with
development of the discipline. This raises the question of whether high
scientific productivity equals large knowledge amount. Here, building on rich
literature on academic conferences and journals, we collect 185 million
articles covering 19 disciplines published during 1970 to 2020, and establish
citation network research area to represent the knowledge flow from the authors
of the article being cited to the authors of the articles that cite it under
each specific area. As a result, the structure formed during the evolution of
each scientific area can implicitly tells how the knowledge flows between nodes
and how it behaves as the number of literature (productivity) increases. By
leveraging Structural entropy in structured high-dimensional space and Shannon
entropy in unstructured probability space, we propose the Quantitative Index of
Knowledge (KQI), which is taken as the subtraction between the two types of
entropy, to reflect the extent of disorder of the citation network in each
discipline. The smaller the KQI, the more the knowledge generated by the
discipline. As a result, the knowledge of each area is reflected objectively
and adatively across different disciplines. With the comprehensive analysis of
all 19 disciplines, the results show that the common understanding that high
scientific productivity equals large knowledge amount is not always true. For
some areas, even though the number of literature is high, the knowledge amount

disciplines follows the long-tailed distribution, where the three areas of

information-related questions. In addition, our analysis reveals the underlying

interface within the $d$-dimensional fractured porous domain, for $d=2, 3$. Two

between the fracture and its surrounding medium: when the permeability in the
fracture is (significantly) larger than in its surrounding medium, it is
considered as a {\it conductive} fracture; when the permeability in the
fracture is (significantly) smaller than in its surrounding medium, it is
considered as a {\it blocking} fracture. The conductive fractures are treated
using the classical hybrid-dimensional approach of the interface model where
pressure is assumed to be continuous across the fracture interfaces, while the
blocking fractures are treated using the recent Dirac-$\delta$ function
approach where normal component of Darcy velocity is assumed to be continuous
across the interface. Due to the use of Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for
the blocking fractures, our numerical scheme allows for nonconforming meshes
with respect to the blocking fractures. This is the major novelty of our model
and numerical discretization. Moreover, our numerical scheme produces locally
conservative velocity approximations and produces approximate solutions that
satisfy the hybrid interface conditions. In addition, our numerical scheme
extends to the case when the blocking fractures intersect each other. Finally,
we provide several numerical examples to demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency

compatibility with the observed data. Those quantifications can then also be
used to choose between hypotheses. While Bayes factors provide an immediate
approach to hypothesis testing, they are highly sensitive to details of the
data/model assumptions. Moreover it's not clear how straightforwardly this
approach can be implemented in practice, and in particular how sensitive it is
to the details of the computational implementation. Here, we investigate these
questions for Bayes factor analyses in the cognitive sciences. We explain the
statistics underlying Bayes factors as a tool for Bayesian inferences and
discuss that utility functions are needed for principled decisions on
hypotheses. Next, we study how Bayes factors misbehave under different
conditions. This includes a study of errors in the estimation of Bayes factors.
Importantly, it is unknown whether Bayes factor estimates based on bridge
sampling are unbiased for complex analyses. We are the first to use
simulation-based calibration as a tool to test the accuracy of Bayes factor
estimates. Moreover, we study how stable Bayes factors are against different
MCMC draws. We moreover study how Bayes factors depend on variation in the
data. We also look at variability of decisions based on Bayes factors and how
to optimize decisions using a utility function. We outline a Bayes factor
toolbox that can be used to implement Bayes factors in practice. We demonstrate

reveal replication effects and to detect publication bias. In conclusion, Bayes

avoids this problem by not requiring explicit error computation and

appear to correspond to aspects of cortex, including the presence of

two kinds of magnetic skyrmions, which can be created and annihilated by
