sembles of coupled oscillators map
to different functional states in a wide range of applications, e.g., active
and resting states in the brain and stable and unstable power grid
configurations. For this reason, explosive synchronization transitions, which
facilitate fast, abrupt changes between these functional states, has recently
seen significant interest from researchers. While previous work has identified
properties of complex systems that support explosive synchronization, these
investigations have been conducted largely on an ad-hoc basis. Here we provide
an exact criterion for explosive synchronization in coupled phase oscillator
ensembles by investigating the necessary relationship between dynamical and
structural disorder. This result provides a critical step towards untangling
the intertwined properties of complex systems responsible for abrupt phase
transitions and bistability in biological and engineered systems.
Furthermore, we find that ensemble methods can provide insights into the
behavior of individual systems, highlighting the importance of large-scale
research in the study of abrupt phase transitions.
  We also find that abrupt changes in clustering coefficient, at the same
structural distance from the system's percolation transition, may indicate
potential bistability in a system, as seen in a mean-field model of a
neural network and exact calculations in a coupled phase oscillator model.
Finally, the clustering coefficient is found to mark the entry into a
second-order synchronization transition, indicating a system where
antiferromagnetic ordering is possible, and where abrupt transitions between
two stable states may represent a change between up and down states in a neural
network.
  These results highlight the importance of investigating the underlying
physics and biology of a system when applying a critical transition framework,
and how movement from a generic complex system architecture to one that is
biologically relevant may have significant benefits for our understanding of
critical transitions in biological and engineered systems.

may have dominated the energy density of the universe and have triggered a
period of matter domination at early times, until their decay before BBN. The

radiation era would imprint observable signatures in stochastic
gravitational-wave backgrounds of primordial origin. In particular, we show how
the detection of the GW spectrum produced by long-lasting sources such as
cosmic strings would provide a unique probe of particle physics parameters.

these GW spectra could be used to derive new constraints on many UV extensions
of the Standard Model. We illustrate this on a few examples, such as
supersymmetric models where the mass scale of scalar moduli and gravitino can
be constrained up to $10^{10}$ GeV. Further bounds can be obtained on the
reheating temperature of models with only-gravitationally-interacting particles,
reaching $10^{10}$ GeV in certain scenarios. Finally, we note that even when
GW signals are not viable to be interpreted in the framework of particle
physics, they could still provide unprecedented constraints on UV theories
assuming that they are generated by the first-order phase transitions induced
by the heavy particles. For that, we illustrate how the transition order and
the particle mass scale can be constrained using the GW amplitude and spectral
shape.

swimmers in Newtonian and viscoelastic (Boger) fluids. By varying the sizes of
the swimmer body and its helical tail, we show that the impact of
viscoelasticity strongly depends on the swimmer geometry: it can lead to a
significant increase of the swimming speed (up to a factor of five), a similar
decrease (also up to a factor of five) or it can have approximately no impact.
Analysis of our data along with theoretical modeling shows that the influence
of viscoelasticity on helical propulsion is controlled by a snowman-like
effect, previously reported for dumbbell swimmers, wherein the front-back
asymmetry of the swimmer leads to a non-Newtonian elastic force that can either
favor or hinder locomotion.
  Our results are relevant for the design of helical robots for various
applications, in particular for tasks in which a high speed is required (as
can be found in medical treatments or naval operations).
  We show that the influence of viscoelasticity depends on the degree of
asymmetry of the swimmer.
  Rigid helical swimmers with a large enough asymmetry perform better (in
terms of speed) in viscoelastic fluids than in Newtonian ones, while those with
a small enough asymmetry lose speed in viscoelastic fluids.
  We suggest that the speed enhancement in highly asymmetric swimmers is due
to the elastic stress that accumulates in the tail during the swim cycle, while
the small asymmetry swimmers lose speed due to the elastic force opposing the
motion.
  We show that the degree of asymmetry that leads to the best speed in
viscoelastic fluids is strong function of the size of the swimmer.
  Moreover, our data suggest that, for a given degree of asymmetry, a optimal
size can exist that leads to the best possible speed.
  Finally, we show that non-Newtonian fluids with higher dimensionless
viscoelasticity (Weber) number lead to better performance (in terms of speed)
than lower-Weber number fluids for highly asymmetric swimmers.
  However, the impact of the Weber number should be fine-tuned based on the
particular swimmer design.
  We also find that the rotation of the swimmer, which is generally expected
to be detrimental to the swimming motion, can also improve the speed (while
keeping nearly the same efficiency).

NN-based inference is more complicated than in traditional methods. This is
because in addition to aleatoric uncertainty associated with noisy data, there

overparametrization, optimization and sampling errors as well as model
misspecification. Although there are some recent works on uncertainty
quantification (UQ) in NNs, there is no systematic investigation of suitable
methods towards quantifying the total uncertainty effectively and efficiently

differential equations and learning operator mappings between
infinite-dimensional function spaces using NNs. In this work, we present a
comprehensive framework that includes uncertainty modeling, new and existing
solution methods, as well as evaluation metrics and post-hoc improvement
approaches. To demonstrate the applicability and reliability of our framework,
we present an extensive comparative study in which various methods are tested
on prototype problems, including problems with mixed input-output data, and
stochastic problems in high dimensions. In the Appendix, we include a
comprehensive description of all the UQ methods employed, which we will make
available as a software bundle for easy implementation and reuse. The present
software notes provide a blueprint for developing a general-purpose
uncertainty quantification software module that can be fine-tuned and tailored
to specific problems in particular.

Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms exploit the information from camera
and inertial sensors to estimate position and translation. Recent deep learning
based VIO models attract attentions as they provide pose information in a
data-driven way, without the need of designing hand-crafted algorithms.
Existing learning based VIO models rely on recurrent models to fuse multimodal
data and process sensor signal, which are hard to train and not efficient
enough. We propose a novel learning based VIO framework with external memory
attention that effectively and efficiently combines visual and inertial
features for states estimation. Our proposed model is able to estimate pose
accurately and robustly, even in challenging scenarios, e.g., on overcast days
and water-filled ground, which are difficult for traditional VIO algorithms to
extract visual features. Experiments validate that it outperforms both
traditional and learning based VIO baselines in different scenes.

slow output frequency, i.e., a few times per second, which are worse than
traditional VIO algorithms. To address this issue, we propose a novel learning
based VIO framework with external memory attention that efficiently processes
inertial signals and combines multi-source information for states estimation.
In this framework, front-end model processes visual streams into feature
extractor, and assigns attention on attention input which combines with the
feature map from feature extractor for pose estimation. With the temporal
smoothness constraint, we fuse the output of front-end with inertial
information for final states estimation. We validate its superiority over
existing learning based VIO studies, and it can outperform traditional VIO
algorithms under various scenes.

parafermion vertex operator algebra
associated to an integrable highest weight module for simple affine Lie
superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$ is studied. Particularly, we determine the generators
for this algebra.
  The study of parafermion vertex operator algebra associated to simple affine
Lie superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$ is an important step for constructing the
corresponding vertex operator superalgebra. In particular, the structure of
this algebra should be needed for constructing operators in 2d conformal
superfield theories (CFT) whose symmetry is given by $osp(1|2n)$. Some
important physical quantities in CFT are related to vertex operators, and the
knowledge of parafermion algebra will greatly benefit for constructing those
operators.
  Simple affine Lie superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$ has a rich structure due to the
large Cartan subalgebra. This fact should influence greatly to the structure
of parafermion algebra. In particular, the Casimir elements of $osp(1|2n)$
play important roles in determining the generators of parafermion algebra.
These elements deploy the role of fermionic basis of the Cartan subalgebra of
$osp(1|2n)$ to map the commutative algebra of bosonic generators to the
abstract basis of the simple modules for $osp(1|2n)$. This approach then
gives a complete set of generators for the parafermion algebra.
  In particular, for $osp(1|2n)$ with $n=4,5$, the study of parafermion
algebra is also related to my previous work on central extension with label
$\hbar$ which appears in certain Casimir operators. The values of $n=4,5$ give
interesting tests on the consistency of the central extension with $\hbar$.
The results then show that the values of $n=4,5$ are consistent with the
definition of the Casimir operators and simple highest weight modules for
$osp(1|2n)$.
  The formal proof for the correctness of all bases used in finding the
generators of parafermion algebra is also given. The proof shows that the
approach of using fermionic basis of the Cartan subalgebra is necessary to
define the correct basis for simple modules of $osp(1|2n)$.

student model for a new task with the help of several decentralized teachers,
whose pre-training tasks and data are different and agnostic. Our motivation
for investigating such a problem setup stems from a recent dilemma of model
sharing. Many researchers or institutes have spent enormous resources on
training large and competent networks. Due to the privacy, security, or
intellectual property issues, they are, however, not able to share their own
pre-trained models, even if they wish to contribute to the community. The
proposed FedSA offers a solution to this dilemma and makes it one step further
since, again, the learned student may specialize in a new task different from
all of the teachers. To this end, we proposed a dedicated strategy for handling
FedSA. Specifically, our student-training process is driven by a novel
saliency-based approach that adaptively selects teachers as the participants
and integrates their representative capabilities into the student. To evaluate
the effectiveness of FedSA, we conduct experiments on both single-task and
multi-task settings. Experimental results demonstrate that FedSA effectively
amalgamates knowledge from decentralized models and achieves competitive
performance to centralized baselines.

through different phases. Once they reach the zero-age main sequence, their
global rotation rate decreases during the main sequence until at least the
solar age, approximately following the empirical Skumanich's law and enabling
gyrochronology. Older solar-type stars might then reach a point of transition
when they stop braking, according to recent results of asteroseismology.
Additionally, recent 3D numerical simulations of solar-type stars show that
different regimes of differential rotation can be characterized with the Rossby
number. In particular, anti-solar differential rotation (fast poles, slow
equator) may exist for high Rossby number (slow rotators). If this regime
occurs during the main sequence and, in general, for slow rotators, we may
consider how magnetic generation through the dynamo process might be impacted.
In particular, we consider whether slowly rotating stars are indeed subject to
magnetic cycles.

magnetic cycles and global polarity reversals for both rotation regimes, but
only if the $\alpha$-effect is saddled on the tachocline. If it is distributed
in the convection zone, solar-type cases still possess a cycle and anti-solar
cases do not. Conversely, we have not found any possibility for sustaining a
magnetic cycle in mean-field models using the helical non-geostrophic $\alpha$
dynamo for fast rotators (super-critical Rossby number). Finally, kinematic
models are particularly suitable for describing the influence of the dynamo
process on bipolar branching and magnetic snowball formation for planetary
mass objects formed around slow and fast rotators.

planetary masses objects that can be formed via the snowball mechanism,
depending on the rotation rate. This implies that some massive planetary
objects might be formed with a magnetic field strong enough to affect their
evolution, in particular by slowing them down. Having a strong magnetic field,
some massive planetary objects might also be responsible for maintaining (or
initiating?) the stellar magnetic field beyond a certain age. Finally, they
may undergo magnetic polarization and magnetic heating when migrating to the
inner boundary of the habitable zone.

Going from the deep interior to the top of the atmosphere, we describe volcanic
outgassing, surface atmosphere interactions, and atmosphere escape.
Furthermore, we address more complex aspects of the history of Venus, including

long-term evolution, and the implications of geochemical and geodynamical

present-day state, based on modeling and observations. In a first scenario, the

second scenario, Venus could have harbored surface liquid water for long

quantum circuits (PQCs), a fact which has inspired recent proposals for
enhancing the performance of TN algorithms using near-term quantum devices, as

combinations of a preexisting analytical decomposition scheme with constrained

runtimes. Our experimental results reveal one particular protocol, involving
sequential growth and optimization of the quantum circuit, to outperform all
other methods, with even greater benefits seen in the setting of limited
computational resources. Given these promising results, we propose that this
protocol could be further improved using recently developed theories of
circuit lower bounds, and might also be of benefit in generating PQC layers for
enhancing TN algorithms using near-term quantum devices.

conservation properties. When properly implemented, conservation of total mass,
energy, and both linear and angular momentum is guaranteed exactly, up to
machine precision. This is particularly important for some applications in
computational astrophysics, such as binary dynamics, mergers, and accretion of
compact objects (neutron stars, black holes, and white dwarfs). However, in
astrophysical applications that require the inclusion of gravity, calculating
pairwise particle interactions becomes prohibitively expensive. In the Fast
Multipole Method (FMM), they are, therefore, replaced with symmetric
interactions between distant clusters of particles (contained in the tree
nodes) Although such an algorithm is linear momentum-conserving, it introduces
spurious torques that violate conservation of angular momentum. We present a
modification of FMM that is free of spurious torques and conserves angular
momentum explicitly. The new method has practically no computational overhead
compared to the standard FMM.

order differential equations and a star formation simulation where matter can
collapse according to the Navier-Stokes equations.
  Finally, we simulate binary neutron star mergers and colliding black hole
systems, and find that our method is at least an order of magnitude more
efficient in preserving angular momentum than the standard FMM.

not employ the first integral of the Euler equation, which is not obtained by
an analytic integration in general. We assign a mass, specific angular momentum
and entropy to each fluid element in contrast to the previous methods, in which
the spatial distribution of the angular velocity or angular momentum is
specified. Those distributions are determined after the positions of all fluid
elements (or grid points) are derived in our formulation. We solve the large
system of algebraic nonlinear equations that are obtained by discretizing the
time-independent Euler and Einstein equations in the finite-elements method by
using our new multi-dimensional root-finding scheme, named the W4 method. To

configurations both barotropic and baroclinic. We also solve three evolutionary

validate that the weak field solution of our formulation is consistent with that

our solution, in contrast to what has been reported in previous studies. We

binary mergers: binary black hole (BBH), binary neutron star (BNS), and neutron
star-black hole (NSBH). For coalescences involving neutron stars, the
simultaneous observation of gravitational and electromagnetic radiation
produced by an event, has broader potential to enhance our understanding of
these events, and also to probe the equation of state (EOS) of dense matter.
However, electromagnetic follow-up to gravitational wave (GW) events requires
rapid real-time detection and classification of GW signals, and conventional
detection approaches are computationally prohibitive for the anticipated rate
of detection of next-generation GW detectors. In this work, we present the
first deep learning based results of classification of GW signals from NSBH
mergers in \textit{real} LIGO data. We show for the first time that a deep
neural network can successfully distinguish all three classes of compact binary
mergers and separate them from detector noise. Specifically, we train a
convolutional neural network (CNN) on $\sim 500,000$ data samples of real LIGO
noise with injected BBH, BNS, and NSBH GW signals, and we show that our network
has high sensitivity and accuracy. Most importantly, we successfully recover
the two confirmed NSBH events, LIGO/GV150914 and LIGO/GV171012, with a
confidence of 94.1% and 89.3%, respectively, using only GW strain data from
real LIGO detectors. Our results demonstrate for the first time that GW
classification using GW strain data is reliable and practical for real LIGO
data.

their circumstellar discs fragment onto multiple self-gravitating objects.
Accretion of these by HMYSO may explain episodic accretion bursts discovered
recently. We post-process results of a previous 3D simulation of a HMYSO disc
with a 1D code that resolves the disc and object dynamics down to the stellar
surface. We find that burst-like deposition of material into the inner disc
seen in 3D simulations by itself does not always signify powerful accretion
bursts. Only high density post-collapse clumps crossing the inner computational
boundary may result in observable bursts. The rich physics of the inner disc
has a significant impact on the expected accretion bursts: (1) In the standard
turbulent viscosity discs, migrating objects can stall at a migration trap at
the distance of a few au from the star. However, in discs powered by magnetised
winds, the objects are able to cross the trap and produce bursts akin to those
observed so far. (2) Migrating objects may interact with and modify the thermal
(hydrogen ionisation) instability of the inner disc, which can be responsible
for longer duration and lower luminosity bursts in HMYSOs. (3) If the central
star is bloated to a fraction of an au by a previous episode of high accretion
rate, the 1:1 orbital resonance may be absent, and objects may cross the inner
boundary in a sequence of roughly equal duration bursts. (4) If the object
identification is based on the density threshold technique, multiple
interactions between objects and the central star may be misinterpreted as
bursts. (5) The burden of the viable burst scenario is that multiple objects
are required to form in the disc.
  We also investigate how the expected episodic accretion can impact the
formation of a HMYSO. In particular, we follow the evolution of a central
proto-star that experiences several bursts. We find that while the standard
definition of the collapse phase is difficult to pinpoint due to the complex
disc evolution, the formation of a HMYSO certainly involves several massive
outbursts, which are required to explain the observed episodic accretion bursts
if the multiple object scenario is sub-dominant. Finally, we discuss the open
questions, such as the object formation efficiency and the diversity of burst
phenomena.

introduced and a maturity adoption level for 5G is assumed.

towers, as well as the measurement protocol to be applied over the ground and

$101 \, \text{dBm}$ for cellular towers, as well as the implementation of
measurement protocols at $100 \, \text{kHz}$ and $1 \, \text{MHz}$ to evaluate

sensor modalities may fail to operate optimally and subsequently provide inapt
input for safe navigation control. In this study, we present an approach for
the navigation of a dynamic indoor environment with a mobile platform with a
single or several sonar sensors using a layered control system. These sensors
can operate in conditions such as rain, fog, dust, or dirt. The different
control layers, such as collision avoidance and corridor following behavior,
are activated based on acoustic flow queues in the fusion of the sonar images.
The novelty of this work is allowing these sensors to be freely positioned on
the mobile platform and providing the framework for designing the optimal
navigational outcome based on a zoning system around the mobile platform.
Presented in this paper is the acoustic flow model used, as well as the design
of the layered controller. Next to validation in simulation, an implementation
is presented and validated in a real office environment using a real mobile
platform with one, two, or three sonar sensors in real time with 2D navigation.
Multiple sensor layouts were validated in both the simulation and real
experiments to demonstrate that the modular approach for the controller and
sensor fusion works optimally. The results of this work show stable and safe
navigation of indoor environments with dynamic objects.

alternative of the conventional PCA has enjoyed great popularity over the past

converges at least linearly to a limiting critical point of the reformulated
problem. Such a point is proved to be a critical point of the original problem
under a condition imposed on the step size. Finally, we conduct numerical
experiments on both synthetic and real datasets to support our theoretical
developments and demonstrate the efficacy of our approach.

optimization solvers. However, the structure of the model (a box-constrained
convex minimization problem) is suitable for using direct methods (i.e.,

paper. The main advantage of such a type of solvers is that they are free from
any nonessential assumptions (e.g., differentiability, smoothness, Hessian
availability), and they can handle large-scale datasets by using parallel
computation. Moreover, having a direct solver is beneficial when implementing
decision support systems, planning, and control applications, where often a
local minimum is sufficient (e.g., in human decision-making processes, or
when the optimal solution is not feasible).

original problem is reformulated in a more general form.

polars, are still relatively poorly understood. An asynchronous polar is a
polar in which the spin period of the white dwarf is either shorter or longer
than the binary orbital period (typically within a few percent). The
asynchronous polars have been disproportionately detected in soft gamma-ray
observations, leading us to consider the possibility that they have
intrinsically harder X-ray spectra. We compared standard and asynchronous
polars in order to examine the relationship between a CV's synchronization
status and its spectral shape. Using the entire sample of asynchronous polars,
we find that the asynchronous polars may, indeed, have harder spectra, but that
the result is not statistically significant.

spectral shape when comparing the asynchronous and standard polars. The
correction factor is shown to be within the uncertainties for the majority of
the sample, indicating that previous results showing a difference in spectral
shape between synchronous and asynchronous polars are likely due to
over-representation of high-state polars in the asynchronous sample.

of asynchronous polars and find that evolution may play a significant role in
the formation of this subgroup.

identify observations necessary to further investigate the role of evolution

topology rather than a global metric map so that only a local metric map is
maintained for obstacle avoidance which ensures the lightweight of the
representation. To guide the robots navigate into unknown spaces, frontiers are
detected and attached to the map as an attribute. We also develop a path
planning module to evaluate the feasibility and efficiency of our map
representation. The system is validated in a simulation environment and a
demonstration in the real world is conducted. In addition, the HiTMap is made
available open-source.

obstacle avoidance, and path planning. Our code provides a feasible

allocation directly on accelerator devices, but all of them suffer from
uncoalesed memory accesses.
  We discovered a broad class of object-oriented programs with many important
real-world applications that can be implemented efficiently on massively
parallel SIMD accelerators. We call this class Single-Method Multiple-Objects
(SMMO), because parallelism is expressed by running a method on all objects of
a type.
  To make fast GPU programming available to average programmers, we developed
DynaSOAr, a CUDA framework for SMMO applications. DynaSOAr consists of (1) a
fully-parallel, lock-free, dynamic memory allocator, (2) a data layout DSL and
(3) an efficient, parallel do-all operation. DynaSOAr achieves performance
superior to state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by controlling both memory
allocation and memory access.

data layout and achieves low memory fragmentation through efficient management
of free and allocated memory blocks with lock-free, hierarchical bitmaps.
Contrary to other allocators, DynaSOAr allocates memory in small, frequent
chunks, like a pool allocator, but with the fully-parallel access of a dynamic
allocator. DynaSOAr supports thread-local allocation as well as parallel
allocation across all threads and provides interfaces to ease implementation of
custom memory layouts. We show that DynaSOAr is versatile by implementing
micro-benchmarks, data-oriented applications, and parallel object-oriented
applications on GPU hardware.

airborne observations. For cloud tomography from space, however, more efficient

acknowledging that optically thick clouds have "veiled cores." Photons
scattered into and out of this deep region do not contribute significant
information to the observed imagery about the inner structure of the cloud. We
investigate the location of the veiled core for the MISR and MODIS imagers.
While MISR provides multi-angle imagery in the visible and near-IR, MODIS
includes channels in the short-wave IR, albeit at a single view angle. This
combination will enable future 3D retrievals to disentangle the cloud's
effective particle size and optical thickness. We find that, in practice, the
veiled core is located at an optical distance of $\approx$5 starting from the
cloud boundary along the line-of-sight. For MODIS' absorbing wavelengths the
veiled core covers a larger volume, starting at smaller optical distances. This
means that effective particle size retrievals from MODIS's short-wave IR
channels need to consider the 3D structure of convective clouds. For MISR, the
veiled core location is independent of particle size, however, it depends weakly
on optical thickness: thinner clouds have a larger veiled core. This indicates
that future MISR 3D retrievals can use the information in the Imagery itself to
correct for the veiled core, without needing additional observations.

fraction of the cloud volume even for relatively thin clouds (i.e. optical
thickness ~2). This means that 3D retrievals need to consider clouds as fully
3D objects, rather than homogeneous clouds with varying optical thickness.
Finally, the contribution of multiple scattering in 3D clouds to the imagery is
non-negligible, even for the relatively thin clouds that are typical in
mid-latitudes.

equilibrium of the ICM is believed to be partially ensured by non-thermal
pressure support, notably the dissipation of energy through turbulent motions.
Accurate mapping of turbulence using X-ray emission lines is challenging due to
the lack of spatially-resolved spectroscopy. Only future instruments such as
the X-ray Integral Field Unit (X-IFU) on Athena will have the spatial and
spectral resolution to quantitatively investigate the ICM turbulence at all
scales. Powerful diagnostics for these studies are line shift and the line
broadening maps, and the second-order structure function. When estimating these
quantities, instruments will be limited by uncertainties of their measurements,
and by the sample variance (aka cosmic variance) of the observation. We extend
here the formalism started in our companion paper I to include the effect of
statistical uncertainties in the estimation of these line diagnostics, in
particular for structure functions. We demonstrate that statistics contribute
to the total variance through different terms, which depend on the geometry of
the detector, the spatial binning and the nature of the turbulent field. These
terms are important when probing the small scales of the turbulence. An
application of these equations is performed for the X-IFU, using synthetic
turbulent velocity maps of a Coma-like cluster observed for 100 thousand
seconds with the GRADES detector. We show that the total variance on the
structure functions is mostly dominated by the statistical uncertainty for the
larger structure functions, while the cosmic variance is usually the most
important source of variance for line broadening and shift maps.

insights into the dynamics of the ICM when observing a single cluster, thanks to
the suppression of the statistical variance. Finally, we emphasise that these
equations can be easily adapted to any spatial line diagnostics of turbulent

perform a unified search over the index. The index construction and search

idea and propose a meta search engine that searches for music lyrics, song
metadata and song audio or a combination of any of these as the input query and

association with molecular outflows, the sample is divided into protostellar
and starless cores. Statistical tests suggest that the protostellar cores are
more massive than the starless cores, even after temperature and opacity biases
are accounted for. We suggest that the mass difference indicates core mass
growth since their formation. The mass growth implies that massive star
formation may not have to start with massive prestellar cores, depending on the
core mass growth rate. Its impact on the relation between core mass function
and stellar initial mass function is to be further explored.

formation in the cloud, since the total mass available for star formation
appears to be $\ga 10^5\, {\rm M}_{\odot}$.

observational evidence for core mass growth, and how it may lead to missing of
similar evidence in other clouds.

the origin of massive star formation, and thus the evolution of galaxies.
However, to demonstrate so, more similar studies on larger samples are needed.

visits, and the information that can be implicitly inferred given explicit data

simultaneously maximize the sensing coverage and sensing reliability, which can
be efficiently solved using a heuristic algorithm to guide the cruising
trajectory of unoccupied RVs sequentially. To validate the effectiveness of the
proposed model, comprehensive experiments and sensitivity analyses are
performed using real-world RV data of more than 20,000 vehicles in New York
City (NYC). Our approach is shown to cover up to 75.5% of all road segments,
which leads to an implicit coverage of 97.2%. More importantly, the proposed
model achieves an average reliability of 87.2% per road segment, which is
critical for supporting various urban transportation analysis and policy
applications.

  This article describes our type-based static verification tool HELMHOLTZ for
Michelson, which is a statically typed stack-based language for writing smart
contracts that are executed on the blockchain platform Tezos. HELMHOLTZ is
designed on top of our extension of Michelson's type system with refinement
types. HELMHOLTZ takes a Michelson program annotated with a user-defined
specification written in the form of a refinement type as input; it then
typechecks the program against the specification based on the refinement type
system, discharging the generated verification conditions with the SMT solver
Z3. We briefly introduce our refinement type system for the core calculus
Mini-Michelson of Michelson, which incorporates the characteristic features
such as compound datatypes (e.g., lists and pairs), higher-order functions, and
invocation of another contract. \HELMHOLTZ{} successfully verifies several
practical Michelson programs, including one that transfers money to an account
and that checks a digital signature.

describe the practical issues that we had to solve in order to establish a
working environment between camlmtc and HELMHOLTZ.

CT denoising thanks to its superior performance despite the fast computational

learning scheme to improve the low-dose CT image quality without requiring
matched high-dose reference data. Unfortunately, one of the main limitations of
the cycleGAN approach is that it requires two deep neural network generators at
the training phase, although only one of them is used at the inference phase.

but the additional memory requirement and increases of the learnable parameters
are the main huddles for cycleGAN training. To address this issue, here we
propose a novel cycleGAN architecture using a single switchable generator. In
particular, a single generator is implemented using adaptive instance
normalization (AdaIN) layers so that the baseline generator converting a
low-dose CT image to a routine-dose CT image can be switched to a generator
converting high-dose to low-dose by simply changing the AdaIN code. Thanks to
the shared baseline network, the additional memory requirement and weight
increases are minimized, and the training can be done more stably even with
small training data. Experimental results show that the proposed method
outperforms the previous cycleGAN approaches while using only about half the
parameters.

networks. Using a single dynamics model, we see clear evidence of task

notably improves performance while using the same amount of parameters. We
illustrate our findings by comparing both methods on a simple gridworld and a
more complex vizdoom multi-task experiment.

ability of the learned model to produce distinct outcomes for different tasks.
We propose to address this issue by using multiple learned models, but this
comes at the cost of increased memory consumption. As a compromise, our
approach of using isolated sub-networks for different tasks provides a practical
solution to the problem and is easy to implement.

Theorem (1933), Godel-Carnap's Diagonal Lemma (1934), and Rosser's
(strengthening of Godel's first) Incompleteness Theorem (1936), whose proofs
resemble much and use almost the same technique.
  For this purpose, we first introduce a general scheme (Lamboas, 1993) of
which these theorems are easy instances. Then we show, via similar proofs, that
their extensions (e.g. Kleene's Incompleteness Theorem, Specker's
Undefinability Theorem, etc.) also fall under this scheme.
  This approach offers a general theory handling these theorems and their
extensions. It simplifies the treatment of these related results and avoids
redundant proofs.
  We end with a few systems to which our scheme does not apply, for which either
the theorem or the proof (or both) are different from the previous ones.
Moreover, we show how our scheme gives another result, not directly related to
FOL systems, interesting on its own.
  Finally, we outline how our scheme could be extended to other areas of logic.
In particular, it should apply to modal and dependent type theories.
  We propose a challenge: decide whether our scheme extends to consistent
quasi-arithmetic theories such as Quine's M32.
  We also report on the difficulty to find a proper generalisation of
Tarski's Undefinability Theorem to richer arithmetics (like computable or
basic recursive geometry).
  Last but not least, we outline on the importance of distinguishing between
theoretical and practical proofs.
  We end with a list of open problems.
  This paper extends the previous work (Lamboas, 1993) on Godel's
Incompleteness Theorems and extends the scope of application of the scheme
illustrating the unity of Godel's first incompleteness theorem, its extensions

applications due to the high atmospheric absorption at THz frequencies,
multi-hop directional transmissions can be enabled to extend the communication

PSR B1133+16, from which we have obtained high-quality dynamic spectra and
their associated scintillation arcs, arising from the scattering screens

individual scattering screens that are responsible for the observed
scintillation arcs, which persist for decades. Using the assumption that the
scattering screens have not changed significantly in this time, we have modeled
the variations in arc curvature throughout the Earth's orbit and extracted
information about the placement, orientation, and velocity of five of the six
screens, with the highest-precision distance measurement placing a screen at

these screens with an under-dense region of the Local Bubble.

longer-time-scale variation in the pulse profile shape and has a much higher

variability in scattering timescales observed in some cases.

Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) is proposed to improve the limited pitch
controllability of vanilla WaveNet (WN) using pitch-dependent dilated
convolution neural networks (PDCNNs). Specifically, as a probabilistic
autoregressive generation model with stacked dilated convolution layers, WN
achieves high-fidelity audio waveform generation. However, the pure-data-driven
nature and the lack of prior knowledge of audio signals degrade the pitch
controllability of WN. For instance, it is difficult for WN to precisely
generate the periodic components of audio signals when the given auxiliary
fundamental frequency ($F_{0}$) features are outside the $F_{0}$ range observed
in the training data. To address this problem, QPNet with two novel designs is
proposed. First, the PDCNN component is applied to dynamically change the
network architecture of WN according to the given auxiliary $F_{0}$ features.
Second, a cascaded network structure is utilized to simultaneously model the
long- and short-term dependencies of quasi-periodic signals such as speech. The
performances of single-tone sinusoid and speech generations are evaluated. The
experimental results show the effectiveness of the PDCNNs for unseen auxiliary
$F_{0}$ features and the effectiveness of the cascaded structure for speech
generation.

attention recently. Most GCNs learn the node representations in Euclidean
geometry, but that could have a high distortion in the case of embedding graphs
with scale-free or hierarchical structure. Recently, some GCNs are proposed to
deal with this problem in non-Euclidean geometry, e.g., hyperbolic geometry.
Although hyperbolic GCNs achieve promising performance, existing hyperbolic
graph operations actually cannot rigorously follow the hyperbolic geometry,
which may limit the ability of hyperbolic geometry and thus hurt the
performance of hyperbolic GCNs. In this paper, we propose a novel hyperbolic
GCN named Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN), which rigorously
guarantees the learned node features follow the hyperbolic geometry.
Specifically, we rebuild the graph operations of hyperbolic GCNs with
Lorentzian version, e.g., the feature transformation and non-linear activation.

centroid of Lorentzian distance. Moreover, we prove some proposed graph
operations are equivalent in different types of hyperbolic geometry, which

distortion to learn the representation of tree-likeness graphs and could enhance
the performance of dense graphs by reducing distortion. LGCN is also robust to
the overfitting problem thanks to the limited number of graph operations.

shows its effectiveness in real-world applications.

the exponential model of delay discounting, without any external driving
force. This may lead to the growth of a rich variety of complex behaviors in
a system of agents.

stimulus, which is related to the addiction problem. Our model illustrates how
the fluctuation in impulsivity due to the random external stimulus affects the
decision-making process of an individual.

from the experiments conducted by Killeen, which furthers validates our model.
Moreover, we show that our approach may be applied to other social systems as
well.

learning and artificial intelligence, where an autonomous system should be
designed to make decisions at the correct time.
  In conclusion, our work illustrates that the Tsallis distribution can be
obtained from the exponential model of delay discounting considering the
fluctuation in impulsivity. This may lead to a richer variety of complex
behavior in a system of agents.

is real one and not just theoretical curiosity. In this brief report, by

calculations may give useful and concrete insights about the negative absolute
temperature to the undergraduate students.

level system ( e.g. the hydrogen atom ) in the negative temperature using the
Dirac's distribution function. Furthermore, we have explained the shift of the
average energy in the negative temperature using the graphical method. This
might be useful to have intuitive understanding of the negative temperature.
Also, we have discussed the non-thermodynamic behavior of the system at the
negative temperature.

intrinsically invreating. The understandable explanation of such a concept may
encourage the young students to continue their pursuit in the science and
engineering.
  Finally, it is worthwhile to say that the negative temperature is not a toy
concept for the theoretical physicists, but also has practical importance. For
example, the negative temperature may be useful to increase the lifetime of the
neutrons in the neutron star.
  In conclusion, the formalism of the statistical mechanics and thermodynamics
may provide convenient tool to understand the concept of negative temperature.

undergraduate students.

applied to explain the other complex concepts in the physics.

weakly-annotated whole slide images? These are two interesting research
questions that we are pursuing and that are reflected in our dataset
format, which includes strongly and weakly annotated images.

has not been studied for speech translation. We attempt to build zero-shot ST

inference. The challenge is that the representation of text and audio is
significantly different, thus the models learn ASR and MT tasks in different
ways, making it non-trivial to perform zero-shot. These models tend to output
the wrong language when performing zero-shot ST. We tackle the issues by
including additional training data and an auxiliary loss function that
minimizes the text-audio difference. Our experiment results and analysis show
that the methods are promising for zero-shot ST. Moreover, our methods are
particularly useful in the few-shot settings where a limited amount of ST data

interpretation of experiments on these materials, which often fall in a regime
of intermediate coupling with respect to electron-electron interactions.

rows (objects) and columns (features). ViDaExpert implements several
statistical methods such as standard and weighted Principal Component Analysis
(PCA) and the method of elastic maps (non-linear version of PCA), Linear
Discriminant Analysis (LDA), multilinear regression, K-Means clustering, a
variant of decision tree construction algorithm. Equipped with several
user-friendly dialogs for configuring data point representations (size, shape,
color) and fast 3D viewer, ViDaExpert is a handy tool allowing to construct an
interactive 3D-scene representing a table of data in multidimensional space and
perform its quick and insightfull statistical analysis, from basic to advanced
methods.

2-D domains is a subject of great importance for the numerical solution of
Poisson's equation and volume integral equations. Complicated domains typically
require discretization by unstructured meshes, over which the direct evaluation
of the potential by quadrature becomes costly. In this paper, we present a
simple and efficient high-order algorithm for computing Newtonian potentials,
based on the use of Green's third identity for transforming the volume integral
into a collection of boundary integrals, which can be easily handled by the
Helsing-Ojala method. As a result, the time cost of the classically expensive
near field and self-interaction computations over an unstructured mesh becomes
roughly the same as the time cost of the FMM-based far field interaction
computation. One of the key components of our algorithm is the high-order 2-D
monomial approximation of a function over a mesh element, which is often
regarded as an ill-conditioned problem, since it involves the solution of a
Vandermonde linear system. In fact, it has long been observed that, when the
function is sufficiently smooth, and when a backward stable linear system
solver is used, the resulting monomial expansion can approximate the function
uniformly to high accuracy. We rigorously formalize this observation in this
paper. The performance of our algorithm is illustrated through several
numerical experiments.
  We also consider the special case of computing potentials relative to a
constant density field. We present a high-order algorithm for this problem,
which is also based on Green's third identity, and is even simpler than the
general algorithm. We also note a remarkable consequence of this problem's
symmetry: the monomial approximation of a function uniformly to high accuracy,
without any need for smoothness assumptions. This is because the symmetry of the
kernel implies that the linear system is symmetric positive definite, and
backward stable solvers for it produce exact solutions up to a scalar factor.
We illustrate this phenomenon through numerical experiments.
  Finally, we consider the computation of potentials in the presence of
boundary conditions of the Neumann type. We present a high-order algorithm for
this problem, based on the use of Green's first identity. We also note a
remarkable consequence of this problem's symmetry: the linear system produced
in the course of deriving this algorithm is symmetric definite, which implies
that, when solved backwards, it produces exact solutions up to a scalar factor,
as demonstrated through numerical experiments
